rv.q: Like some forgotten treasure found in the attic, the Old Vic‘s radiant revival of “The Winslow Boy” — now presented on Broadway by the Roundabout Theater — practically glows in the dark.
A trivial crime makes for delightful revival.
Rest assured, though, that you'll come away with a proper appreciation of how good "The Winslow Boy" is.

Reticence may be a fundamental characteristic of his plays, but whether the figures onstage here articulate their feelings or not, their devotion, their sacrifice and the convictions that guide them make The Winslow Boy unexpectedly moving.

Theatre Company has wisely imported much of the show from The Theatre in London, including a handsome set and costumes by Peter McKintosh as well as Lindsay Posner's crisp direction, which finds real humor in a play where jeopardy, though localized, is very present.
There is great pleasure in being handled with authority by a playwright who knows what he's doing.
Watching Parry and Nivola stiffly dance around each other’s feelings is melanchic and delightful.
As the emotional stakes of Arthur’s campaign are gradually revealed, “The Winslow Boy”
Drawing-room drama is rarely this inviting.
Scrupulously acted and handsomely designed, the show vibrates with humor and genuine emotion.
Led by Roger Rees, the entire company in this beautifully staged historical British drama is top shelf!
Lindsay Posner's elegant staging heightens the spring-wound tension Rattigan skillfully builds.

So why waste any more time before declaring that what Rattigan advocates Haimes and Posner have worked out is one of the best productions on which the Roundabout has ever raised a curtain at the Theatre?
The failure to stage the climactic courtroom scene is actually one of Rattigan's finest touches.
The surprising humor, and the vibrant and detailed performances of the cast offer so much more juice than the more overtly relevant play.
The truth, while more complicated, is no harder to predict than any of the developments in Winslow Boy; but this winsome revival will charm you nonetheless.
But there’s only so much you can do with the material, which feels like an over-long and decidedly twee Masterpiece Theatre drama.
Here, it comes off as stale and stiff drawing-room fare that only springs to life whenever Roger Rees, who plays the father, seizes the stage in a fit of passion.
But it appears that the beating heart of this piece was left on the other side of the pond.
